md_solver:
What pursuit adds is reconstruction, and it costs identification. With 64 atoms each on the same states:

| solver | largest write identified | FVU of a refit on its atoms |
|---|---|---|
| OMP | 0.647 | 0.180 |
| one-shot ranking | 0.766 | 0.533 |
| one-shot ranking through the dual frame | 0.801 | 0.531 |
| LASSO | 0.849 | 0.433 |

OMP reconstructs best and identifies worst. So the paper's 65% is OMP's limit, not the dictionary's.
md_sae: **Reviewers MgDZ and 7MWE: SAE features, as vectors no prompt produced.** I decomposed all 24,576 decoder directions of the residual SAE of Bloom (2024) for this layer over the same dictionary. The first atom chosen is an MLP row for 93% of features, against 54% for random directions. Sixteen atoms leave 0.48 of a feature unexplained, against 0.72 under the rotated dictionary and 0.47 for a typical state. So in this dictionary a feature looks like a state, not like a single write, and its nearest write is usually an MLP neuron. Whether the recovered writes are as interpretable as the features is still untested.
md_oracle:
**Reviewer NMa5: ground truth for the attention and embedding atoms.** I built the oracle you describe. Each head's true write, projected on that head's own basis atoms, gives a true coefficient for every attention atom. For the embeddings, the only true writes are the token's own row and its own position row. On typical states, with the 64-atom OMP support:

| part of the support | share | against ground truth |
|---|---|---|
| MLP rows | 62% | 35% are real writes (Section 4.2) |
| attention atoms | 21% | sign right for 70%, against 50% by chance |
| token-embedding rows | 17% | 0.3% are the current token |
| position rows | 0.1% | 0.2% are the current position |

The head that wrote the most has an atom in the support for 20% of tokens, or 28% with centred writes, against 14% for a random head. The token's own embedding row is selected for 3% of tokens. So the non-MLP atoms, 38% of the support, should not be read as attributions.
